foodDescription: Lamb or beef stewed for hours with potatoes, onions and carrots until the potatoes break down and thicken it. Named after lobscouse, a sailors’ stew, and the source of the city’s nickname. Eat it with pickled red cabbage or beetroot and buttered bread.

Scouse with no meat in it, made at the end of the week or the end of the money from potatoes, onions, carrots and stock. Still cooked at home and in some cafés. Thinner than the real thing and not pretending otherwise; the pickled cabbage does the work.

A dense slab of bread pudding or leftover cake, packed with dried fruit and soaked in syrup until it sags. The name is usually traced to Lord Nelson, via a richer Nelson cake. Heavy, sticky and cheap, a bakery staple. Eat it warm, with custard if offered.

Hard butter toffee first sold in the 1700s by Molly Bushell in Everton, then a village above the docks. It gave Everton FC its nickname, the Toffees, and before home games a Toffee Lady still throws Everton mints, striped boiled sweets, into the crowd.

A shortcrust tart filled with a whole lemon, peel and all, cooked down with brown sugar, butter and egg. Sharper and darker than a French lemon tart, with a faint bitterness from the rind. An old home recipe, now mostly found in cookbooks and the odd café.

Chips fried crisp, then tossed in a wok with salt, chilli, onion, peppers and five-spice. Liverpool’s Chinese takeaways claim them, and the city has Europe’s oldest Chinese community, so the claim holds up. Eat them fast, before the steam turns them soft.

Steamed dumplings, char siu pork buns and egg tarts in the restaurants around Nelson Street in Chinatown, under its ceremonial arch. The community dates to the 1860s, when the Blue Funnel shipping line began sailing to China. Go at weekend lunchtime.

The Friday tea from the chip shop: fish or a pie, chips, mushy peas and, here, curry sauce or gravy over the top. Many chippies here are Chinese-run, so the curry sauce is the takeaway kind. A chip butty, chips in a buttered roll, is the cheap option.

Minced beef, onion and potato in shortcrust, the matchday lunch around the football grounds. The best known come from Homebaked, the co-operative bakery on Oakfield Road opposite Anfield, Liverpool FC’s stadium. On match days they sell out before kick-off.

The two old Liverpool beers. Higsons bitter was the city’s pint for generations until the brewery closed in 1990; the name has since been revived. Cains brewed at the red-brick brewery on Stanhope Street. Try one in a Victorian pub like the Philharmonic.

Plain, dry, flaky crackers made by Jacob’s at its Aintree factory, north of the city, since 1914, near the racecourse where the Grand National is run. Eaten with butter and cheese. Trying to eat several without a drink is an old playground challenge.

Tiny brown shrimps from the sands off Southport, a seaside town north of the city, packed into pots under butter spiced with mace and nutmeg. Spread on hot toast so the butter melts. A Victorian seaside treat, still at fishmongers and on older menus.

White bread, butter and strawberry jam, folded or cut in half; a butty is any sandwich here. Comedian Ken Dodd, from the Knotty Ash district, spent a career joking about the jam butty mines worked by his Diddy Men. Best with a mug of tea.

Asparagus grown in the sandy coastal soil at Formby, north of Liverpool, a market-garden crop there for over a century. The season is short, roughly May and June. Eat it simply, with butter or a soft egg, and buy it from farm stands while it lasts.

Hard, flat ginger biscuits sold at the market in Ormskirk, a Lancashire market town just north of the city, where they have been made since the 1700s. Sold by the bag. They snap rather than bend and are best dunked in tea, the ginger arriving slowly.
